summary: Children compose 2-D shapes — combining triangles, squares, trapezoids, and half-/quarter-circles into composite shapes and finding new shapes within them. The goal is to move along Clements & Sarama's trajectory: from unsystematic trial-and-error assembly (Piece Assembler), through trial-and-error picture making, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION — choosing a piece because its angle and side length will fit, using turns and flips intentionally, and decomposing a composite back into the simpler shapes that make it up. The core teaching medium is manipulating flat pieces into outline (puzzle) tasks engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, with immediate fit/misfit feedback.
misconceptions: Assembles by trial and error with no advance plan and does not anticipate the new shape (an expected early trajectory level, not a fault).
Chooses pieces by general shape only, not by matching angles and side lengths, so pieces do not fit the gap.
Sees the composite as one whole and cannot decompose it into the simpler shapes it is made from.

activities.title: Fill the outline with the right pieces
steps: Give the child flat shape pieces (for example, pattern blocks, tangram pieces, or cut-out triangles, squares, rectangles, trapezoids, half-circles and quarter-circles) and an outline puzzle card that those pieces can cover exactly. Standard pattern blocks and tangrams do not include half-circles or quarter-circles, and tangrams have no trapezoid, so add cut-out pieces for any shapes the set lacks.
As they work, ask them to say which shape they are using and why.
Before each placement, prompt: 'Will this piece fit this gap? How do you know?' — encouraging a prediction from the gap's edges and corners.
When a piece doesn't fit, have them compare the gap's edge length and corner angle to the piece, then choose one that matches.
Let them use turns and flips to make a piece fit, naming what they did ('I flipped it so the slanted edge lines up').
activities.insight: A piece can be chosen in advance by matching its side length and angle to the gap, rather than by trying pieces at random until one happens to fit.

activities.title: Same pieces, different shapes
steps: Using two congruent right-isosceles (tangram-style) triangles, have the child join them along their long (hypotenuse) edges to form a square. Then have them rejoin the same two triangles along one of the shorter equal edges, mirrored so the two right-angle corners sit side by side, to form a larger triangle instead. Joining them along a shorter edge with one triangle turned the other way makes a parallelogram, which is another new shape worth naming. (Note for the adult: two equilateral pattern-block triangles would instead make a rhombus, not a square, so choose right-isosceles triangles for this square example.)
Have them put two half-circles together to form a circle, and explore what else the pieces can make.
Ask: 'You made a square from two triangles — can you make a different shape with those same two pieces?'
activities.insight: The same pieces can compose different shapes depending on how they are turned and joined — composing is a deliberate, reversible act.

activities.title: Find the shapes hiding inside
steps: Show the child a completed composite shape and ask 'Which smaller shapes are hiding inside this?'
Have them lift and separate the pieces to reveal, for example, that the square is made of two right-angled (right-isosceles) triangles or the circle of two half-circles.
Ask them to name each component shape as they take the composite apart, then rebuild it.
activities.insight: A composite shape is built from — and can be pulled apart into — simpler named shapes; seeing the whole does not mean you can only see the whole.

activities.title: Reference and post-check (supporting activities)
steps: As a reference, show a composite alongside a reveal of its decomposition ('this is made of two triangles') to support naming the parts.
As a post-check after hands-on building, have the child match composites to the component pieces that make them, or sequence which pieces make a given shape.
Use a short spoken prediction before a build: 'Which piece will fit here, and why?'
activities.insight: Naming and matching parts consolidates vocabulary and checks understanding, but the composing skill itself is built through the hands-on fitting activities above.

checkQuestion: Here are pattern-block pieces — triangles, squares, trapezoids and some half-circles and quarter-circles. Cover this outline puzzle exactly using the pieces, and as you work tell me which shapes you are using. Then show me two triangles making a square, and tell me one other shape you could make from the pieces.
checkAnswer: Selects pieces by their attributes and places them to fill the outline exactly, choosing pieces with anticipation rather than only trial and error; combines two triangles into a square (and, e.g., two half-circles into a circle); and decomposes and renames the composite by its component shapes.
